Package Overview

Elham Ebrahimi

Source: vignettes/Package-Overview.Rmd
Package-Overview.Rmd

Introduction

camtrapReport provides a reproducible workflow for turning standardised camera-trap data into structured ecological reports. It brings data-quality checks, ecological summaries, visualisation, and report generation together so that users can move from a Camtrap DP dataset to a documented report without having to assemble each step separately.

The workflow starts with camData(), which creates a camReport object from the input data. The same object is then used to generate two main outputs:

  • a Data Status Check, created with status(), which helps users identify issues in the data before interpretation or analysis; and
  • an Ecological Report, created with report(), which combines selected analyses, figures, tables, maps, and explanatory text in a single document.

Input data

The main input is a camera-trap dataset in Camtrap DP format, supplied either as a ZIP archive or as an extracted Camtrap DP directory.

Optional supporting data can also be provided. These include habitat information and a study-area boundary, which can be used in relevant summaries, maps, and ecological analyses.

data currently takes a file path, rather than an in-memory list or data frame. habitat accepts a data frame, and study_area accepts a spatial file, terra::SpatVector, or sf object. A Camtrap DP contains datapackage.json plus linked deployment, media, and observation tables. Deployments describe camera placements and their active periods; media rows describe photographs or videos; observations describe classifications derived from those media. An event (also called a sequence) groups related media within a time interval; it is not necessarily one photograph or one animal. See the standard’s field definitions.

There is no universal converter for arbitrary camera-trap tables in this package. Export Camtrap DP from the original management platform when possible, or map your tables and metadata to the Camtrap DP specification. The camtrapdp package supports reading, editing, and writing existing Camtrap DP objects. camtrapReport’s readiness checks do not replace the standard’s full schema-validation workflow.

One camReport stores one study-area boundary. In the GUI, multiple uploads are the component files of one shapefile (.shp, .shx, .dbf, .prj, etc.), not a separate boundary for each year. When the boundary changes between years, use separate year-specific Camtrap DP subsets and objects with the matching boundary; use separate directories so their caches remain separate. The optional camtrapdp::filter_deployments() and camtrapdp::write_camtrapdp() functions can help prepare those subsets while preserving links to media and observations.

Optional taxonomy enrichment

camData(..., enrich_taxonomy = TRUE) preserves the previous default: when the optional taxize package is installed, a fresh import sends scientific names to GBIF to supplement taxonomic classes and missing orders. A message announces those requests. For offline work or confidential species lists, disable this enrichment explicitly:

cm <- camData(data_path, update = TRUE, enrich_taxonomy = FALSE)

This disables GBIF taxonomy requests, not network operations in subsequently selected modules or map backgrounds. Imported names, families, supplied orders and observation counts are retained. When taxonomic classes are unavailable, automatically defined class-based groups such as birds, reptiles, amphibians and wild_mammals are not created. Their group summaries can therefore be absent, while order-based groups such as large_mammals remain usable when the source supplies the relevant orders. Reusing a cache does not remove enrichment already stored in that object; update = TRUE is needed to import again with a different setting.

Cached inputs and re-importing

camData() saves the processed object as __camReport_Object.rds beside the extracted dataset. With the default update = FALSE, a later call using that directory still reuses the saved object. New caches include a lightweight snapshot of the four selected source files: datapackage.json, deployments.csv, media.csv and observations.csv. Their relative paths, sizes and modification times are recorded before parsing, so later changes during a long import do not become a falsely fresh post-import snapshot.

On reuse, added or removed core-file candidates in the dataset root or known input directories, or changed source sizes/times, trigger an advisory warning. The cached object is still returned: it is not automatically rebuilt, deleted or rewritten. Older caches without a snapshot warn that freshness cannot be verified. After editing source data, rebuild explicitly with camData(data_path, update = TRUE) and resupply optional inputs and the intended taxonomy setting before regenerating reports.

This is a metadata check, not content hashing or a full provenance guarantee. Same-size edits whose modification time is restored can be missed. It does not recursively search previously unknown nested directories, or detect changes to optional habitat data and study-area boundaries supplied separately. Use update = TRUE after changing those inputs even if no warning appears.

Bundled example data

The package includes a relationship-preserving subset of the GMU8_LEUVEN Camtrap DP dataset for examples, demonstrations, and automated tests. It contains eight derived camera locations, 87 deployments, 15,492 retained media records, and 11,092 observation records. Bundled habitat data and a derived study-area boundary provide optional inputs for exercising those parts of the workflow. The subset is a software fixture and should not be used for ecological inference; its provenance and transformations are documented in inst/external/README-Leuven-dataset.md in the source repository.

Key outputs

Data Status Check

The Data Status Check is intended to help users inspect the quality and completeness of a dataset before moving on to ecological interpretation. It summarises issues such as missing information, annotation and validation status, temporal inconsistencies, spatial outliers, observation types, and other aspects of data readiness.

It is generated with:

status(cm, filename = file.path(tempdir(), "overview-status.html"))

The report is diagnostic rather than inferential: passing the checks does not mean that a sampling design is suitable for every ecological analysis. The check tables support user judgement; there is no computed overall quality grade or automatic gate preventing ecological report generation. Correct problems in the source Camtrap DP, recreate the object with camData(data_path, update = TRUE), and rerun status(). The report does not modify the source CSV/JSON records for you. camData() caches the processed object as __camReport_Object.rds and, when a boundary is supplied, study_area.map in the extracted dataset directory.

Ecological Report

The Ecological Report brings together selected ecological summaries, analyses, figures, tables, maps, and explanatory text in an article-style document.

It is generated with:

report(cm, filename = file.path(tempdir(), "overview-report.html"))

The content of the report depends on the selected sections, available data, and analytical settings. Users can therefore adapt the report to the purpose and scope of a particular monitoring project.

The standard profile uses pooled multi-year REM parameters. The EOW profile uses the population_density_annual module and estimates REM parameters independently for each species and sampling year. New report objects use an OpenStreetMap-first online background, with automatic fallback through OpenStreetMap Germany and OpenTopoMap, then a neutral grid if all fail. This default is intended for noncommercial research reports and needs no additional settings. Free access does not remove the services’ usage terms or attribution requirements, and online availability cannot be guaranteed. Existing explicit background settings are retained; cm$setting$map_basemap <- "offline" disables tile requests. Local file:// reports start with Germany because they cannot send Standard’s required web Referer; serve the HTML over HTTP(S) to try Standard first. A single bad tile does not discard a usable background. Each provider has a bounded loading deadline and is attempted at most once; ecological overlays and controls remain available when every provider fails. See the map-background guide for policies, attributions and explicit CARTO/Esri modes.

Apart from the resolved-destination notice, HTML and PDF rendering is quiet by default. For troubleshooting, enable console-only progress and stage/chunk timings with options(camtrapReport.progress = TRUE); set it to FALSE afterwards to return to normal rendering. Warnings, errors and notices about omitted content remain visible. These diagnostics do not change report content or analytical calculations.

Shiny is used for the optional gui() interface; the code-based workflow does not need a running Shiny application. Optional analysis packages are declared by the YAML modules and can be installed through an explicit call to install_all() after inspecting those requirements.

The GUI initially suggests a valid project root returned by the optional here package, otherwise falling back to the object’s valid dataset directory. Check that this is your intended location and choose an existing output directory. It previews the resolved paths and does not change the R working directory. Its overwrite checkbox starts unchecked, protecting existing reports, R Markdown sources and saved objects until replacement is explicitly allowed.

Both status() and report() create a rendered file together with the intermediate .Rmd source used to render it. The resolved paths are displayed before rendering. With a filename that contains no directory, the object’s existing dataset directory is used. Otherwise supply a filename including an existing output directory. An invalid directory is an error, not a reason to silently use getwd() or another location.

Existing rendered output and the same-stem .Rmd file are protected by overwrite = FALSE, the default. Choose a new filename or explicitly set overwrite = TRUE to replace them. HTML and PDF outputs with the same stem share the .Rmd path, so use distinct stems when retaining both versions. A .pdf filename or format = "pdf" creates a static browser-printed PDF through the optional pagedown package; Chrome or Edge is also required. PDF reports do not include a table of contents. The module registry’s formats column identifies modules that support html, pdf, or both; report generation omits incompatible modules and dependent children for the requested output. Printable tabsets are expanded for PDF so every panel remains visible. Executed package examples copy the bundled data and write generated reports to temporary directories.

Working with the camReport object

The camReport object keeps the input data, metadata, settings, and report outputs together during the workflow. For most users, the important point is that the same object can be inspected, adjusted, and then used to regenerate reports with updated settings.

For example, metadata can be viewed or changed with info():

info(cm)

info(cm, name = "authors")

info(cm, name = "authors") <- c(
  "Elham Ebrahimi",
  "Patrick Jansen"
)

Users can also change the taxonomic focus, select years, adjust filters, or choose which report sections should be included before regenerating the report.

A modular reporting workflow

camtrapReport is modular in the sense that a report is assembled from separate sections rather than from one fixed template. Users can keep only the sections relevant to their data and reporting needs, and can omit or reorder sections when needed.

For example:

# Inspect available report sections
section_names()

# Keep only selected sections
n <- section_names(
  keep = c(
    "introduction",
    "methods",
    "study_area"
  )
)

# Apply the selection
sections(cm, n)

# Generate the report
report(cm, filename = file.path(tempdir(), "overview-selected-report.html"))

For repeated report types, a named profile stores an ordered selection without moving or duplicating module YAML files:

# Inspect bundled or user-registered profiles
profile_names(cm)
section_names(object = cm, profile = "default")

# Apply a profile when rendering
report(
  cm,
  profile = "default",
  filename = file.path(tempdir(), "overview-default-report.html")
)

# A profile may also select status modules for the status report
sections(cm, profile = "default", report_type = "status")

The two module pools are the ecological modules in reportSections and the data-status modules in statusSections. Profile entries use report::module or status::module to identify a pool explicitly. This also allows selected status modules to be placed in an ecological report profile. See the Report profiles guide for creating, applying, and sharing profiles.

This makes it possible to use the same overall workflow for projects that differ in species, survey duration, spatial extent, available covariates, or reporting objectives.

Users who want to develop or manage additional report modules can find more detail in the Module management and extension guide.

Reproducibility, interpretation, and scope

camtrapReport supports reproducible reporting by applying a consistent workflow from data checking through ecological analysis to report generation. Analytical modules use established ecological and statistical methods, with default settings that provide a common starting point across camera-trap datasets.

Because the workflow is modular, users can select relevant analyses and adjust module-specific settings, species groups, and thresholds according to their data, study design, and analytical objectives. Results should therefore be interpreted in relation to the characteristics of the dataset, sampling design, and assumptions of the selected methods.

General guidance on recording computational environments and managing reproducible research workflows is available from the Reproducible Research CRAN Task View.

Relationship to other camera-trap packages

camtrapReport is intended to complement, rather than replace, existing camera-trap and ecological analysis packages. Different packages address different parts of the workflow.

Area Examples Relationship to camtrapReport
Standardised camera-trap data camtrapdp camtrapReport uses Camtrap DP as its main input format.
Data management and exploration camtrapR, ct, camtraptor These packages provide complementary tools for preparing, exploring, and summarising camera-trap data.
Activity, diversity, abundance, and density analyses activity, overlap, iNEXT, camtrapDensity, Distance Specialised methods can support individual analyses used within a reporting workflow.
Hierarchical and spatial modelling unmarked, secr These packages provide specialised modelling frameworks outside the main reporting role of camtrapReport.

The main role of camtrapReport is therefore not to reproduce every specialised method. Its focus is on bringing data checks, selected ecological analyses, visual outputs, metadata, and explanatory text together in a consistent report generated from a standardised dataset.

Conclusion

camtrapReport provides a structured workflow for moving from standardised camera-trap data to quality-checked and reproducible ecological reporting. Its modular design allows the workflow to be adapted to different datasets, monitoring objectives, and analytical needs.

For more detail, see the Data Status Check, Ecological Report, and Module management and extension articles.
